REUTERS/Nina Liashonok MOSCOW, Nov 8 (Reuters) – Russia said on Sunday overnight strikes by its forces had hit three cargo vessels that were carrying military goods for Ukraine and two electricity substations, which it said supplied power to the Ukrainian defense industry. The Defence Ministry said Russian forces had struck a container ship delivering weapons and military equipment to the Black Sea port of Odesa, and another in the port of Chornomorsk, which is in the same southwestern region of Ukraine. According to the ministry, the second container ship had delivered dual-use cargo to Ukraine. It said a third vessel, a dry cargo ship hit south-west of Odesa, was carrying weapons and military equipment for Ukraine’s armed forces. Reuters could not independently verify the ministry’s claims. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine. The ministry also said Russia had hit two power substations in Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk and Zhytomyr regions, both of which it said powered military-industrial enterprises. Ukrainian power company DTEK said a Russian overnight attack on energy facilities in Dnipropetrovsk had left more than 600,000 people without electricity. “Important energy facilities in the region were damaged in an overnight attack,” the company said on Telegram. articles.title: CMA CGM updates surcharges across Africa and Canada outbound trades
articles.summary: CMA CGM has announced new and revised freight surcharges covering several trade routes connecting Asia with Africa, as well as shipments from Canada’s West Coast to the Indian Subcontinent, Middle East Gulf and Red Sea. The adjustments include Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) on selected African routes and a Rate...
articles.body: CMA CGM has announced new and revised freight surcharges covering several trade routes connecting Asia with Africa, as well as shipments from Canada’s West Coast to the Indian Subcontinent, Middle East Gulf and Red Sea. The adjustments include Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) on selected African routes and a Rate Restoration Initiative (RRI03) for shipments originating from western Canada. Implementation dates range from November 10 to December 3, 2026. New surcharges on Asia–Africa routes CMA CGM will introduce a PSS of US$400 per TEU for all cargo shipped from South China to Mozambique, effective November 10, 2026, based on the loading date. The surcharge will remain in effect until further notice. The carrier has also announced a revised PSS of US$500 per TEU for dry and reefer cargo moving from Southeast Asia to West Africa. This adjustment will apply from November 15, 2026, and is specifically applicable to short-term contracts. Additional changes will affect shipments from China to Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, and Mombasa, Kenya. For cargo originating in South China, a PSS of US$400 per TEU will take effect on November 10, 2026. The same amount will apply to shipments from North and Central China beginning November 15, 2026. CMA CGM noted that the surcharge for shipments originating in China will be subject to filing with the Shanghai Shipping Exchange and/or may be included in the ocean freight rate. Rate restoration measures for Canadian exports Separately, CMA CGM will implement a new Rate Restoration Initiative, designated RRI03, for shipments from Canada’s West Coast to destinations in the Indian Subcontinent, Middle East Gulf and Red Sea. The adjustment will take effect on December 3, 2026, and will apply in addition to previously announced Rate Restoration Initiatives. For shipments to the Middle East Gulf and Red Sea, the increase will be US$1,000 per 20-foot container and US$2,000 per 40-foot or 45-foot container. For cargo moving to the Indian Subcontinent, the amounts will be US$600 per 20-foot container and US$1,200 per 40-foot or 45-foot container. Both adjustments cover all cargo types except Open Top and Flat Rack equipment. CMA CGM stated that the announced adjustments are separate from applicable base ocean freight rates. Additional charges, including bunker-related surcharges, terminal handling charges and other local or contingency fees, may also apply. The latest measures follow earlier freight surcharge announcements across several Asia–Africa trade corridors, reflecting further adjustments to CMA CGM’s pricing structure on selected international routes.

articles.body: Tankers: VLCC Market Cools Down in Hellenic Shipping News 09/11/2026 T he tanker market has witnessed a decline over the course of the past week. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Affinity said that “VLCCs have softened throughout the week as limited enquiry and increasingly competitive Suezmax alternatives have tempered owners’ expectations. East of Suez, there was a small but noticeable increase in activity in an area with a tight prompt tonnage list. However, this proved insufficient to prevent rates from easing, with a Fujairah-East fixture rumoured to be on subs at WS 565 and TD34 now sitting at WS 545”. According to Affinity, “the Atlantic saw sharper declines as cheaper Suezmax cover drew business away from VLCCs, with Brazil-East falling from WS 607 on Monday to WS 572 on Wednesday and WAFR-East falling to WS 500 today. Tighter prompt tonnage could offer some support East of Suez if enquiry continues, while Atlantic VLCCs face a tougher task securing cover as long as smaller tanker classes remain cheaper. After a couple of weeks of weak levels of Suezmax activity and an ever-growing tonnage list, rates were always set to correct downwards, but the speed at which they have dropped has been stark. In WAFR, rates have softened to WS 400 last done, down from approximately WS 700 at the start of the week”. “CPC rates have also seen a sharp decline, with WS 725 on subs following a very brief return to the conference rate of WS 900 owing to AWRP artificially inflating rates. The US Gulf has also seen a steep correction downwards, with WS 295 now on subs for TA, a decrease from theoretical levels of WS 550, as witnessed in one deal! Rates out of Guyana, meanwhile, have remained untested this week, but the last done of WS 625 does not look repeatable, and it is likely that it will follow the rest of the Atlantic down the slide. East of Suez, things have remained quiet as charterers continue to favour VLCCs; one cargo did emerge, however, with Fujairah-East now paying at WS 535. But given the plethora of tonnage out East, one can expect a long caravan of ships ballasting west to have emerged come Monday morning. The Mediterranean Aframax market weakened this week. Monday opened quietly after a subdued close last Friday, with a long position list and weak sentiment encouraging charterers to test rates lower. By Tuesday, they had capitalised on the tonnage supply to push levels down, and Wednesday brought lacklustre activity with all western markets under pressure. Thursday saw rates slide in 100-point steps on every fixture, leaving charterers firmly in control and further drops still expected. TD19 ends the week at WS 285”, the shipbroker said. Meanwhile, “it was a similar story in the North Sea, where Aframax rates softened through the week as sharp corrections in surrounding markets made their way into that one. On Monday, lengthy local lists left charterers with the advantage, and Tuesday saw charterers keep enquiries close and conduct off-market fixing. Owners spent Wednesday digesting a sharp correction while charterers pressed for less. By Thursday, with Med and USG rates falling and the entire Atlantic Basin under pressure, TD7 looked overpriced, and further downside is expected. The rate is WS 325 at the time of writing”, Affinity noted. Meanwhile, in the product tanker segment, the shipbroker commented that “the AG LR2 market has taken some losses this week. Once again, the throughput of CPP to the market depends largely on one Gulf State oil company, and there has been good activity from this area. But with so few chartering conduits to shipowners, there were freight discounts off the back of a positions list longer than what the market has been used to through summer and autumn. 75,000 T naphtha was agreed last week at WS 450, but this week the rate was adjusted sharply down to WS 400. Westbound deliveries were looking poised to go under USD 10 Mn, and it has happened, with USD 9 Mn on subs for Oman-UK Cont via Bab-el-Mandeb. EAFR was also re-adjusted down from 90 x WS 485, with 90 x WS 400 on subs at this time of writing”. articles.title: Asia-US container rates largely stable; liquid tanker rates steady to higher
articles.summary: Rates for shipping containers from east Asia and China to the US were largely stable this week while rates for liquid chemical tankers ex-US Gulf were steady to higher. articles.body: Asia-US container rates largely stable; liquid tanker rates steady to higher in International Shipping News 09/11/2026 Rates for shipping containers from east Asia and China to the US were largely stable this week while rates for liquid chemical tankers ex-US Gulf were steady to higher. Rates to the West Coast edged higher on the low end and are between $7,540-8,340/FEU (40-foot equivalent unit) while rates to the East Coast fell slightly on the low end and are between $9,300-11,500/FEU, remaining near the highest since mid-2022 for both routes. Rates from supply chain advisors Drewry were flat from Shanghai to Los Angeles and fell by 3% from Shanghai to New York, as shown in the following graph. Drewry said congestion at Chinese ports has begun to ease with average vessel waiting times at Shanghai improving to 35 hours last week as weather conditions improved and demand softened. Carriers are still controlling capacity with blank sailings, and Drewry said there were three scheduled for the coming week, down from five this week, indicating an increase in effective capacity. Thus, Drewry anticipates rates remaining under downward pressure and could fall in the near term. Weekly rates from online shipping marketplace and platform provider Freightos were essentially flat to the West Coast and fell by 6% to the East Coast. Judah Levine, head of research at Freightos, said it is unclear if general rate increases (GRIs) announced by carriers for 1 November will go through. He said some freight forwarders think the increases are unlikely to stick as the transpacific trade lane finally enters slow season. Rates on the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI), which tracks rates for containers leaving Shanghai, fell by 1.46%, the first decrease after four weeks of increases. Rates on the NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) rose by 1.3% to the West Coast and fell by 0.2% to the East Coast. Container ships and costs for shipping containers are relevant to the chemical industry because while most chemicals are liquids and are shipped in tankers, container ships transport polymers, such as polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP), which are shipped in pellets. Titanium dioxide (TiO2) is also shipped in containers. They also transport liquid chemicals in isotanks. LIQUID CHEM TANKERS US chemical tanker freight rates assessed by ICIS were stable to higher this week, with increases on the US Gulf (USG) to ARA trade lane and mostly unchanged on all other major shipping routes. Along the USG to ARA route, there has been an uptick in activity this week along with steady contract volumes continuing to be seen in the market. As a result, space remains tight, pressuring rates higher, and should linger for the foreseeable future. On the spot side it remains somewhat active as several traders have inquired about space and as acetic acid, ethanol, methyl tertiary butyl ether (MTBE), methanol, and styrene continue to dominate this trade lane. Although, the number of fixtures remain somewhat limited due to a limited number of available ships leaving rates pressured higher. Similarly, from the USG to Brazil, COA (contract of affreightment) cargoes continue employing a sizable part of the tonnage, providing support for the market. Overall, the market remains very challenging, and spot rates remained steady on this trade lane. Only a few inquiries were seen in the market, and several owners have parcel space available on both the East and West coasts, but this should be completed quickly. Additionally, the CPP (clean petroleum products) market remains strong into the region, leaving fewer vessels available for the chemical sector. As a result, rates are seeing upward pressure but remain steady for the time being. The usual methanol and caustic soda cargoes are the most frequently seen in the market. Along the USG-to-India route, quotations have been very limited. Overall demand seems to have slowed from the activity seen in previous weeks. Fewer methanol and monoethylene glycol (MEG) cargoes have been reported in the market this week. On the USG-to-Asia route, COA volumes continue to dominate any available tonnage, therefore rates remain steady, with little sign of easing in the near term. However, there could be upward pressure as most owners are looking to fill any available space. Activity in the market was driven primarily by larger methanol cargo movements, which made up most of the vessel-fixing activity. Meanwhile, demand for smaller chemical parcel shipments remained subdued, indicating weaker interest in smaller-volume cargoes. articles.body: Dry Bulk Market: Capesizes End The Week on Firmer Note in International Shipping News 09/11/2026 C apesize The Capesize market experienced a mixed but ultimately firmer week, with an initial period of weakness giving way to improved sentiment and firmer conditions, although momentum remained uneven across the basins. The Pacific was the main source of pressure early on, with C5 falling from $13.80 to the low $13.00s as two miners remained active but consistently tested lower levels. Despite a midweek recovery in sentiment, activity remained selective, with Friday’s miner business concluded at $13.25, leaving the route below Monday’s opening levels. The South Brazil and West Africa to China markets saw a more pronounced turnaround, recovering from a lack of demand and bids in the early part of the week to a notably active Wednesday when more than 15 C3 fixtures were reported, pushing rates towards $37.00. However, the subsequent slowdown and lower fixtures on Thursday suggested owners were becoming more cautious. The North Atlantic remained the relative outperformer, with stronger transatlantic business lifting the C8 index to $41,000 by Friday, and fresh enquiry emerging across both TA and FH routes. Lower bunker prices also provided some support to TCE earnings towards the latter part of the week. Overall, the market finished the week on a firmer footing, with the BCI 182 opening at $35,944, dipping on Tuesday before recovering steadily to close at $39,395. Panamax-Kamsarmax The market began the week on a subdued note before gathering momentum as improving demand and tightening tonnage availability supported firmer sentiment across both basins. In the Atlantic, transatlantic and fronthaul enquiry gradually increased, with rates strengthening as tonnage availability tightened, particularly off the West Mediterranean. However, the North Continent remained comparatively well supplied, limiting broader gains. An 82,000-dwt fixed a transatlantic trip at just below $30,000 basis delivery EC South America, while US Gulf fronthaul business was reported at $24,000 basis North Continent delivery and an EC South America fronthaul fixed at $18,750 basis delivery West Coast India. The Pacific also gained ground, supported primarily by healthy Australian mineral demand, with an 82,000-dwt fixing at $22,000 to South China, a 90,000-dwt fixing at $24,000 to Japan, and an 81,000-dwt fixing at $20,500. Indonesian activity remained steady, with a 76,000-dwt fixing at $17,000 for a trip to South China. North Pacific conditions showed signs of stabilising, although increasing tonnage availability tempered optimism, with an 82,000-dwt fixing at $19,750 for a round trip to Japan. Period activity remained limited, with an 83,000-dwt reportedly fixing for 11–13 months at around $19,500. Ultramax/Supramax A subdued week with a few holidays and Eisbein this week saw rates under pressure. North America managed to turn the tide and rates began to recover with two 63,000-dwt vessels reported for petcoke to India at $34,000 and $34,500, and a 52,000-dwt achieving $28,000 from Port Arthur to Iskenderun with petcoke, having seen a 63,000-dwt fixed for grains to China at a disappointing $27,000 via Cape of Good Hope earlier in the week. Continent activity was greatly reduced compared to previous weeks, although a 60,000-dwt still agreed a strong $36,000 basis delivery Tilbury for scrap to the East Mediterranean, and the Mediterranean was also slow albeit with relatively low tonnage availability. The south Atlantic appeared devoid of early stems, although demand for end November/early December looked healthier. After supporting the market for weeks, Asia also saw increased tonnage with NoPac grains slowing and backhaul trades unable to support the market any longer, with a 63,000-dwt fixed from North China to West Africa with steels/generals at $26,000, whilst Southeast Asia saw tonnage from India/Chittagong increasingly competing and pushing rates lower. The Indian Ocean was hit hardest as it was bereft of fresh enquiry, with rates under severe pressure, with a 57,000-dwt fixed from Richards Bay to Pakistan with coal at $21,500 plus $215,000 ballast bonus. There was very little period chat, however a 61,000-dwt open West Coast India for mid-November was rumoured fixed for one year in the $18,000s. Handysize The market remained generally quiet over the week, with limited fixing information and mixed regional sentiment. The Continent and Mediterranean gained support from fresh activity and tightening tonnage. A 36,000-dwt vessel open Constanza on 2–5 November was fixed for a trip via the Black Sea to Poland with urea at $12,250. The US Gulf also showed signs of strengthening as improving cargo flows and a shortage of prompt tonnage supported sentiment. A 39,000-dwt vessel open Wilmington was fixed for delivery Savannah in mid-November for a trip to the Continent with pellets at $21,000. By contrast, the South Atlantic remained soft throughout the week, with limited fresh demand keeping rates under pressure and prompting both owners and charterers to lower their expectations. A 28,000-dwt vessel open Tema on 1–7 November was fixed for a trip via Recalada to Algeria with grains at $14,000. In Asia, activity remained muted and rates were broadly flat, with little clear direction. A 35,000-dwt vessel open Thailand was placed on subjects for a trip to Japan in the $18,000s. articles.body: IMO Council urges stronger protection of seafarers amid threats to global shipping in International Shipping News 09/11/2026 Council condemns attacks on merchant shipping in the Red Sea and Black Sea, mourns loss of 25th seafarer since onset of Strait of Hormuz conflict, and renews Secretary-General’s tenure. The Council of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has reaffirmed its commitment to protecting the safety, security, health and well-being of seafarers amid continuing threats to international shipping. Meeting for its 138th session at IMO Headquarters in London (2–6 November 2026), the Council reiterated that vital shipping lanes should remain open, safe and secure. It underscored that seafarers must be protected wherever they are and whatever their nationality, including in geopolitical disputes over which they have no control. Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez emphasized: “Seafarers continue to lose their lives, suffer serious injuries, face abandonment, are denied repatriation and are deprived of basic human necessities, including water, food and medical care, resulting from the ongoing geopolitical conflicts.” He highlighted the death of another seafarer this week, following an attack on the M/T VELOS SAPPHIRE in the Strait of Hormuz on 5 November, bringing the number of confirmed casualties to 25 since the conflict in the Middle East began. In total, at least 130 attacks against commercial vessels in the region have been verified by IMO, with thousands of seafarers at risk, including those on ships that have been unable to leave the Persian Gulf. ​The 138th session of the IMO Council was chaired by Mr. Victor Jimenez of Spain (pictured above, right, with IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez). The Council called on Member States to refrain from unlawful measures that would jeopardize the safety of seafarers and international shipping. The Secretary-General further committed to finding additional concrete measures IMO can take to help prevent further loss of life and alleviate the human cost of the crisis. Global maritime security challenges The Council strongly condemned attacks carried out by the Houthis against merchant and commercial vessels and their crews in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait, as well as attacks by the Russian Federation against merchant vessels, seafarers, port infrastructure, search and rescue assets and other maritime safety services supporting the operation of Ukraine’s special maritime corridor. It reiterated its commitment to the security and freedom of navigation in the Black Sea. The Council noted the increase in piracy and armed robbery attacks in the Western Indian Ocean and Gulf of Aden region, including 17 instances of attempted and actual piracy and armed robbery at sea in this region alone since the start of the year. It noted the work underway to address these developments, within the framework of the Djibouti Code of Conduct and its Jeddah Amendment. The Council requested the Secretary-General to continue monitoring maritime security developments in these various regions and to keep Member States informed. Other key decisions Renewal of the Secretary-General’s mandate The Council decided to renew the mandate of IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Domínguez for another four-year term, concluding on 31 December 2031, and to make a recommendation to the 35th regular session of the IMO Assembly, in accordance with Article 22 of the IMO Convention. 2027 IMO Gender Equality Award The Council decided to award the 2027 IMO Gender Equality Award to Ms. Yu Jiajia, nominated by China, in recognition of her significant personal achievements in overcoming barriers to women’s participation in the maritime sector. The award will be presented to Ms. Yu on 18 May 2027 (Women in Maritime Day). The Council also endorsed the recommendation to award a Letter of Commendation to Ms. Gemma Griffin, nominated by Denmark. Revised Rules of Procedure approved The Council approved revised Rules of Procedure of the Council, related to suspension or adjournment of meetings, suspension and closure of debates, voting, and the concept of a point of order. It invited other IMO organs to consider the amendments with a view to harmonizing their respective Rules of Procedure with those of the Council. Funding approved for IMO digital platforms The Council approved the Secretary-General’s funding proposal to complete the upgrade of the IMO’s Global Integrated Shipping Information System (GISIS) and develop an e-Learning platform, in an initial amount of GBP 2 million. With respect to additional funding requirements, the Council requested the Secretary-General to present detailed cost estimates, implementation timelines and recurring expenses for both initiatives to a future session of the Council. Member States contributions to the Organization The Council noted the status of Member States’ contributions to the IMO’s General Fund and the Working Capital Fund, with a collection rate of 97.62%. The Council urged Member States with outstanding contributions to fulfil their financial obligations to the Organization in full and at the earliest possible opportunity. Next Council session The Council noted the proposed dates for its 139th regular session, to be held at IMO Headquarters in London from 19 to 23 July 2027. articles.summary: MEPC 85 is coming up fast, and negotiations for what the Net Zero Framework will look like are increasing in intensity. articles.body: The IMO NZF as agreed upon in 2025 still remains the most likely way to achieve the IMO 2023 GHG strategy in International Shipping News 09/11/2026 MEPC 85 is coming up fast, and negotiations for what the Net Zero Framework will look like are increasing in intensity. With several proposals on the table, it is likely that the outcome will be a composite, blending together different aspects of each proposal – although none of the new ideas have improved the entire regulation impact and the NZF as agreed upon in 2025 still remains clearly the most likely way to achieve the revised 2023 GHG strategy. Any policy that is adopted needs to continue to support the IMO’s GHG goals. With each operational component of the NZF subject to separate negotiations, it is important to ensure the overall goals of the GHG Strategy are achieved. UCL and Rocky Mountain Institute have conducted a sensitivity analysis on structural elements of the NZF, focusing on GFI trajectories and compliance prices (Remedial Units or Direct Contributions), as well as measuring the impact of differing ZNZ fuel reward schemes. This work has informed the recent Institute of Marine Engineering, Science & Technology (IMarEST) submissions (ISWG-GHG 23/2/9, 23/3/7, and 23/3/8 – see below). We have found (unsurprisingly) that higher ambition GFI trajectories with higher RU prices results in lower cumulative emissions. RMI/UCL Shipping and Oceans Research Group modelling has clarified: Even slightly loosening the GFI trajectory leads to higher cumulative emissions. The GFI trajectory effectively sets the emissions allowed, making it one of if not the centerpiece of the entire policy; with negotiations considering loosening of the trajectory, there is possibility of undermining the entire purpose of the NZF as even slightly loosening the trajectory results in higher near-term emission while making later emission reduction more expensive and disruptive. Lowering the price of Remedial Units leads to a rapid increase in cost of abatement and impact on states. RUs can be seen as a measure of the incentivisation of investment in alternative energy: the higher the RU price, the stronger the investment in solutions that reduce emissions and therefore the lower the cost of abatement. We tested the ‘as-is’ prices (RU1 = $100 and RU2 = $380) held constant, versus a scenario where the RU2 price starts at $380 increases over time (broadly reflecting the rising cost of emissions abatement as lower-cost measures are exhausted); only with RU price increasing was investment and energy transition sustained, leading to cost-effective emission reduction. We also considered ‘No RU’ scenario reflected policy that only trades SUs for compliance, but included vessel impoundment as an enforcement mechanism. To represent the significant impact of impoundment, we modeled RU2 as $1,000 – showing that there is still an effective price on emissions in this policy design even if it is not labelled as such. Because the modelling assumes long-run equilibrium in prices, this policy still achieves emission reduction, but in practice the policy design creates high risks of disruption and high transport costs as volatility and price shocks in the energy system would be more directly translated into shipping price shocks than if there was a third compliance mechanism (RU price etc.) The proposed ‘Direct Contributions’ are an alternative to RUs where shipping companies make payments to qualifying projects instead of paying the IMO; however, there is a possibility that companies will recover their contribution in the backend if they have financial stake in the project. We refer to this as ‘leakage’. We modeled this possibility by assuming an RU pricing scheme of 50/190, reflecting a 50% recovery of contributions. In every scenario, this led to substantially higher cumulative emissions than NZF ‘as is’, and much higher cost of abatement – as well as no IMO GHG fund for addressing JET. ZNZ incentives of any kind must be differentiated by fuel type (e-fuels and biofuels) to achieve climate goals Policies structured where incentives were not differentiated led to a massive increase in the use of biofuels and higher use of fossil fuels in the 2050 fuel mix compared to differentiated incentives. Regional policies have included both rewards and multipliers successfully, but differentiate them to adjust to climate benefits and cost. For example, FuelEU utilizes multipliers, and the proposed ETS revision’s SMAP mechanism differentiates rewards by different proportions of each alternative fuel’s cost gap to conventional fuels. Overall, the Net Zero Framework as-is reflects elements that result in lower emissions, lower costs of abatement and therefore impacts, as well as stable revenues for both ZNZ and JET – diverging from its specification compromises one or more of these outcomes. While different elements of the policy are under negotiation, we must recognize that deviating from what was agreed upon could undermine its fundamental purpose. Source: UCL and Rocky Mountain Institute 2026-11-09 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Any policy that is adopted needs to continue to support the IMO’s GHG goals.
With each operational component of the NZF subject to separate negotiations, it is important to ensure the overall goals of the GHG Strategy are achieved.
This work has informed the recent Institute of Marine Engineering, Science & Technology (IMarEST) submissions (ISWG-GHG 23/2/9, 23/3/7, and 23/3/8 – see below).

articles.body: Drewry: Intra Asia Container Index Down Last Week in International Shipping News 09/11/2026 Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI) declined by $26 to $1,478 per 40ft container. However, spot rates across intra-Asia trade remained uneven. While rates on routes such as Shanghai–Singapore and Ho Chi Minh City–Shanghai increased, others recorded declines amid improving port congestion and easing operational constraints. This divergence highlights the continued volatility in regional freight markets. See detailed commentary below. IACI decreases as congestion improves • The Drewry Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI), the benchmark widely referenced by procurement teams, declined by $26 to $1,478 per 40ft container. However, spot rates across intra-Asia trade remained uneven. While rates on routes such as Shanghai–Singapore and Ho Chi Minh City–Shanghai increased, others recorded declines amid improving port congestion and easing operational constraints. This divergence highlights the continued volatility in regional freight markets. • Spot rates from Greater China to Northeast, Southeast and South Asia recorded mixed performance this week. Following several weeks of severe port congestion caused by typhoons and operational disruptions, conditions at major Chinese ports have started to improve, contributing to rate declines on the Shanghai–Jakarta and Shanghai–Busan routes. Rates to Jakarta fell 8% to $2,538 per 40ft container, while those to Busan declined 2% to $1,132 per 40ft container. Average vessel waiting times at Shanghai eased from 36 to 35 hours, while Qingdao recorded a sharper improvement in vessel waiting time from 35 to 23 hours as of Week 44. In contrast, congestion at major transhipment hubs, particularly Singapore, intensified, pushing Shanghai–Singapore rates up 9% WoW to $2,064 per 40ft container. Meanwhile, the deteriorating situation in the Middle East continued to keep Shanghai–Jebel Ali rates elevated at $8,199 per 40ft container. Drewry expects rates to remain broadly stable in the coming weeks. However, resilient underlying demand continues to attract additional capacity participants and prompt leading carriers to introduce new services, thereby adding to market volatility. • Spot rates across Southeast and Northeast Asian trade routes recorded an unusual mixed performance this week, with rates showing opposite trends. Jakarta–Shanghai rates increased 11% to $90 per 40ft container, while Jawaharlal Nehru Port (JNPT)–Shanghai rates declined 6% to $79 per 40ft container. Meanwhile, OOCL is set to launch its new China–Indonesia Service (CIS4) on 22 November 2026, further strengthening connectivity between the two countries. The service will connect Qingdao, Shanghai and Nansha with Jakarta and Surabaya, with a port rotation of Qingdao – Shanghai – Nansha – Jakarta – Surabaya – Singapore – Qingdao. The additional service will provide customers with more direct shipping options and enhance OOCL’s network coverage across the China–Indonesia trade. • Geopolitical tensions and weather-related disruptions remain key risks for intra-Asia trade, as port closures and vessel delays could constrain available capacity and exert upwards pressure on freight rates. Escalating tensions in the Middle East have added to market volatility, with the US carrying out another round of limited strikes against Iran, targeting Qeshm Island this week. The elevated bunker costs and persistent US–Iran tensions continue to support freight rates. The Intra-Asia Container Index is already around 135% higher than a year earlier, highlighting the extent of the increase in regional shipping costs. Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI) reports actual spot container freight rates for major intra-Asia trade routes. articles.body: UK P&I Club takes measured 2027 P&I premium renewal position as it continues plans to reinforce resilience and support for Members in Marine Insurance P&I Club News 09/11/2026 The Board of the UK P&I Club has agreed a 4.5% General Increase for the 2027 policy year reflecting continuing claims inflation and the rising cost and complexity of major casualties. The Club’s 2026/27 performance remains in line with expectations. Pool claims have been relatively benign during this period, and whilst retained claims have been higher than forecast year to date, the positive development on prior-year claims means the Club forecasts a year-end combined ratio of approximately 100%, an improvement on 2025/26. Investments have also generated sound returns and the Club continues to be very strongly capitalised, with free reserves of more than US$600 million. Building on this financial strength, the Club and TT Club jointly acquired Thomas Miller Holdings in October 2026, bringing the management under Club control and retaining more value for Members. The acquisition forms part of the wider transaction that will bring the Clubs together on 20 February 2027, subject to regulatory approval. Combining the Clubs’ complementary strengths will create the first transport mutual to span the full cargo supply chain. Current market conditions reinforce the rationale for the merger, which will create greater scale, even stronger financial resilience and more capacity to invest in claims handling, loss prevention and specialist expertise. Inflation continues to impact underlying loss costs, particularly for illness and injury claims. The Club also sees major casualties becoming more complex and costly, with salvage, environmental response, wreck removal and third-party liabilities able to rise well ahead of general inflation. Upward pressure is also expected on the cost of the International Group reinsurance programme for 2027. Premiums need to keep pace with claims costs, but the Club’s financial strength and the benefits of the merger have enabled the Board to keep the General Increase to 4.5%. Individual renewals will reflect each Member’s record, risk profile and existing terms. The Club will also target a 10% increase in deductibles below US$50,000, subject to a minimum increase of US$1,000. William Beveridge, Chief Underwriting Officer, UK P&I Club, said: “The General Increase reflects the continuing rise in underlying claims costs. Pool claims have been relatively benign this year, but major casualties are becoming more expensive and complex, and the cost of illness and injury claims continues to rise. The Club’s financial strength, and the expected future benefits of the merger, allow us to take a longer-term view, keeping the General Increase to 4.5% while recognising that premiums need to cover the inflationary increase in the cost of claims. “The Club is in a robust position. We expect to improve our combined ratio this year, our investments continue to perform well, and our capital base remains among the strongest in the International Group. This sets firm foundations for our strategy to grow and diversify. Our merger with TT Club is a key part of that strategy, and today’s market complexity highlights its relevance. Together we will have greater scale and even stronger financial resilience, with more capacity to invest in the expertise and support our Members rely on as their risks change.” Source: UK P&I Club 2026-11-09 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Hapag-Lloyd has announced a series of freight rate adjustments covering shipments from Pakistan, the Middle East, Asia and Oceania to destinations in the Arabian Gulf, North America and West Africa. The measures include two Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) and a General Rate Increase/General Rate Adjustment (GRI/GRA), with implementation dates ranging from November 6 to December 1, 2026. The changes apply to different container types and trade corridors, with charges calculated either per container or per twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU). Reefer surcharge for Pakistan–Arabian Gulf shipments Hapag-Lloyd will introduce a Peak Season Surcharge of US$500 per container for refrigerated cargo moving from Karachi and Port Qasim in Pakistan to selected Arabian Gulf destinations. The surcharge applies to 20-foot reefer containers and 40-foot high-cube reefer containers, with effect from November 16 through November 30, 2026. The destinations covered are the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Oman, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar. North America rate adjustment and Tema surcharge The carrier has also announced a GRI/GRA of US$1,000 per container for shipments from the Indian Subcontinent, Pakistan and the Middle East to North America. The adjustment covers 20-foot and 40-foot dry, reefer and special containers, including high-cube equipment. It will apply to containers gated in full from December 1, 2026, and will remain in effect until further notice. Separately, Hapag-Lloyd has announced a PSS of US$400 per TEU for cargo shipped from Asia and Oceania to Tema, Ghana. This surcharge applies to all container types and takes effect for cargo loaded on board from November 6, 2026. It will remain applicable until further notice. The three announcements introduce different charges across several trade routes, with shippers advised to consult Hapag-Lloyd’s applicable tariffs for further details.

articles.body: Kuehne+Nagel has announced three senior management appointments across the United States, Germany and Southern Europe, with the changes taking effect between November 2026 and January 2027. Daniel Randig has been appointed National Manager for the United States, effective 1 November 2026. Meanwhile, Björn Traemann will take over as National Manager for Germany on 1 January 2027. Miguel Germano will also assume the position of Cluster Manager for Spain, Portugal and Malta from 1 January 2027. The appointments involve experienced executives who have held management positions across several international markets and logistics divisions. New leadership across key logistics markets Daniel Randig brings nearly three decades of experience in the logistics industry, covering sea freight, air freight, sales and general management. He joined Kuehne+Nagel in Brazil in 2001 and subsequently held positions in the United States and the Middle East. Most recently, he served as National Air Logistics Manager for the US. Randig succeeds Marcus Bennett, who will move into a new global management role within the company. Björn Traemann has worked for Kuehne+Nagel for more than 23 years. His experience includes international leadership and Sea Logistics positions across Germany, China, Singapore, the Middle East, Belgium and Luxembourg, and Vietnam. He succeeds Tobias Jerschke, who is leaving Kuehne+Nagel after more than 28 years to pursue opportunities outside the logistics industry. Meanwhile, Miguel Germano brings 18 years of international management experience with the company. He previously held leadership positions in Portugal and Turkey before becoming National Manager for Mexico, his most recent role. Germano succeeds Miguel Ambielle Fernandez, who will also assume a new global management position within Kuehne+Nagel. According to the company, the appointments form part of its approach to developing internal leadership and drawing on international market experience. The announcement did not specify any accompanying changes to Kuehne+Nagel’s freight forwarding services or operational network.

On Sunday, Saudi Arabia’s energy ministry said an administrative building belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco in Riyadh had been damaged by falling debris after an attempted attack, with no injuries or fatalities reported. Qatar , which has been mediating in talks to try to end the conflict that has shaken the world economy, on Saturday denied reports that the US and Iran had failed to reach a deal. The Qatari prime minister had affirmed that both sides were continuing ?to ?work toward an agreement, it said. Iran has submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday, saying the US was reviewing it but discussions would depend on Washington first meeting Tehran’s seven demands. These include sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and war reparations, while Washington insists nuclear issues must feature in initial talks. By Lucia Kassai, Devika Krishna Kumar, Charles Gorrivan and Archie Hunter Nov 8, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Oil traders are seeking approval from the US government to use some tankers that were sanctioned for their involvement in shipping illicit oil, in an effort to address a vessel crunch and lower prices. At least four companies, including Trafigura Group, Vitol Group, Mercuria Energy Group Ltd., and Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. are in discussions with US officials for licenses that would allow them to purchase or lease some ships that are blacklisted by the US government, according to people with knowledge of the matter. The move comes as the Trump administration tries to lower oil prices that spiked after the US and Israel launched their war on Iran, triggering the worst supply disruption in history. Freight rates, a major component in the final price of oil, surged to a record in recent weeks amid tanker shortages and the risks of sailing through the Strait of Hormuz. Ships have been forced to take on longer voyages to secure supplies and charterers have been forced to cough up higher insurance fees. Last month, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the administration is working with investors who buy idled sanctioned tankers, refurbish them and use the ships to transport non-sanctioned oil. The idea is to convert “ dark tankers to legitimate tankers ,” he said. Treasury officials are reviewing applications and may issue authorizations on a case-by-case basis, rather than a blanket exemption, said the people, asking not to be named discussing private information. The talks cover about 50 of the roughly 1,600 ships currently sanctioned by the US . No decision is final and the timeframe for approvals is unclear, the people added. Representatives for ADNOC, Trafigura, Mercuria and Vitol declined to comment. The applications include supertankers, the oil industry’s largest vessels, able to transport 2 million barrels, some of the people said. The cost to send US oil to Asia in a supertanker climbed to nearly $40 a barrel in early October, up from $5, a year earlier. While rates have since softened, they remain near historical highs, contributing to oil prices that are hovering around $100 a barrel. To be sure, any licenses from the US Treasury or the Office of Foreign Assets Control would only apply to vessels sanctioned by the US. The European Union and the UK have imposed significant restrictions on Russian and Iranian oil, and targeted the so-called “shadow fleet” used to circumvent restrictions on Russian energy exports. It’s also unclear how much the measure would ultimately lower prices. The Trump administration has unleashed a series of measures aimed at lowering soaring energy costs for American consumers, including releasing millions of barrels from emergency reserves and waiving some fuel-related laws. Still, pump prices remain stubbornly elevated and were a major contributing factor to the Republican Party’s staggering losses in the midterm elections this week. The effectiveness at lowering prices will also depend on the profile of the ships rehabilitated. Repurposing tankers that had been previously idled — such as the tanker named Skipper , which has been sitting off the coast of Texas since December — would have a greater impact than just changing the status of vessels operating in the dark fleet, one of the people said. Related Article: U.S. Seizure of Shadow Fleet Tanker ‘Skipper’ Ends Years-Long Sanctions-Evasion Run While most of the sanctioned ships are older than the mainstream fleet, raising concerns about maintenance and safety, they could still be used in short-distance trips such as between the US and the Caribbean or Latin America, freeing newer tankers for long-haul voyages, the person said. The challenge for the Trump administration is to boost shipping capacity and lower oil prices while trying to prevent bad actors from get an influx of cash. As of Nov. 4, there are 1,568 ships hit by US sanctions, including 462 crude oil tankers, according to Treasury data compiled by Bloomberg. Most remain under the radar of enforcement authorities, typically switching off their satellite location signals. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.body: Ellerman City Liners has integrated Viasea Shipping into its European shortsea operations, bringing the two companies under a unified operational framework. The move follows Ellerman’s acquisition of the Norwegian shortsea operator from ColliCare Holding in November 2025. Since then, the companies have worked to align their operations, schedules and customer services. The combined network connects the United Kingdom, Norway, the Netherlands, Poland and Lithuania with other European markets. It is supported by rail, road and inland transport services across Northern Europe. Ellerman said customers will gain access to coordinated schedules, aligned operating systems and a wider range of multimodal transport options through a single provider. REUTERS/Loren Elliott By Vallari Srivastava and Sumit Saha Nov 6 (Reuters) – The Iran conflict has sent tanker rates soaring, forcing sellers to deepen discounts on heavy crude grades and giving US Gulf Coast refiners a cost advantage over Asian rivals, executives said after reporting bumper third-quarter profits. Security threats around the Strait of Hormuz, a key maritime chokepoint through which about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies passed before the war started, have disrupted tanker traffic, while higher war-risk insurance premiums and longer voyages have driven upshipping costs. The disruption particularly benefited US Gulf Coast refiners, which could buy discounted heavy crude produced closer to home, including from Canada and Venezuela, while Asian rivals faced sharply higher freight and insurance costs to import similar grades through longer and riskiershipping routes. US refining margins more than doubled in the third quarter. Rising freight costs have widened discounts on Canadian heavy crude, including Western Canadian Select (WCS), which typically trades below US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI), creating a windfall for Gulf Coast refiners, as more than 70% of their facilities are configured to process heavier crude. “The main story right now in the market is freight rates,” Randy Hawkins, vice president of Crude And Feedstocks Supply And Trading at Valero Energy VLO.N, said on a post-earnings conference call. Freight costs for shipping crude from the US Gulf Coast to Asia have jumped to $30-$35 a barrel from about $5 a year earlier, Hawkins said. “Higher freight rates actually give us an advantage into the typical export markets into Latin America,” said Gary Simmons, chief operating officer of Valero, adding that it mainly competes with European barrels in that market. Ample heavy crude supplies from Canada and Venezuela , combined with elevated freight rates, have widened the WTI-WCS differential, lowering feedstock costs, US refining executives said. For Phillips 66 PSX.N, every $1 widening in the WCS-WTI differential is worth about $140 million in gains, Brian Mandell, executive vice president of marketing and commercial, said. Higher shipping costs have also been more than offset by stronger fuel margins, said Delia He, an oil and tanker market analyst at Arrow Shipping. “For every extra dollar of freight, the diesel margin has grown by at least eight,” He said. POSITIONED FOR A STRONG 2027 US refiners have also been shielded from the impacts of higher spot tanker rates following the war due to their advance shipping arrangements. Phillips 66 said it had secured more than 40 time-charter vessels before the Iran conflict , covering about 40% of its asset-based shipping needs. Valero, PBF, Marathon and Canada’s Suncor SU.TO also secured chartered fleets before the war began, insulating them from the surge in prices. Wider differentials are expected to continue to lend strength next year as well, some industry executives said. Top US refiner Marathon Petroleum MPC.N expects record Canadian heavy crude processing in the fourth quarter, while CEO Maryann Mannen has said that margins are expected to remain elevated through at least mid-2027. “In the near term we will take advantage of it,” HF Sinclair DINO.N said of the wider discounts, adding, “we do see the differentials stay wider than they have throughout the near term, at least through 2027.” (Reporting by Vallari Srivastava and Sumit Saha in Bengaluru; Editing by Liz Hampton and Shinjini Ganguli) (c) Copyright Thomson Reuters 2026. (Photo: Evos via Port of Hamburg) India’s Adani Ports and Special Economic Zone (APSEZ) has agreed to acquire Netherlands-based liquid storage operator Evos B.V. in a €2.56 billion ($2.88 billion) deal that will give the company a major foothold in Europe’s energy and fuel storage market. Evos is Europe’s second-largest independent liquid storage operator, with eight port-based terminals across the Netherlands, Germany, Spain, Belgium and Malta. Its facilities have a combined storage capacity of 6.3 million cubic meters across 452 tanks, supported by 63 vessel and barge berths and extensive pipeline connections. Evos handled 37 million metric tons of liquid cargo in 2025, including gasoline, gasoil, marine fuels and jet fuel. Its portfolio also includes emerging fuels such as sustainable aviation fuel, biofuels, methanol and bioethanol. The acquisition marks a significant expansion of Adani’s international operations, extending its global footprint to 28 ports and terminals across 10 countries upon completion. “Evos marks an important milestone in APSEZ’s trajectory towards handling 1 billion tons of cargo and building a truly global, integrated transport platform,” said Karan Adani, managing director of APSEZ. The acquisition also gives Adani greater exposure to Europe’s evolving fuel market as demand grows for alternative marine and aviation fuels. Adani Ports, India’s largest private port operator, has been expanding internationally through investments in port infrastructure and logistics. Its existing overseas operations include terminals in Sri Lanka, Israel, Tanzania and Australia. The transaction carries an equity value of €1.18 billion and will be financed through debt, subject to regulatory approvals and works council consultation. MUFG has provided financing commitments of up to €2.8 billion for the proposed transaction. The companies did not announce an expected closing date. REUTERS/Juan Carlos Hernandez The Trump administration has expanded sanctions targeting Cuba’s maritime and energy sectors, identifying five Cuban-flagged vessels as blocked property and opening the door to further sanctions against foreign companies operating in the country’s marine industry. The measures, announced Thursday by the State Department , target eight companies and two individuals accused of supporting the Cuban government through petroleum shipments, offshore business networks and military procurement. The action also includes a new Treasury Department determination allowing sanctions against foreign persons operating in Cuba’s marine, manufacturing, electronics and technology sectors. Among those targeted is Cyprus-based Caroil Transport Marine Ltd., which manages Cuban-flagged tankers involved in transporting energy products. The company was previously sanctioned in 2019 under U.S. measures targeting Venezuela. Three vessels associated with Caroil were identified as blocked property: the crude oil tanker Esperanza , chemical and products tanker Gloria C , and products tanker Maria Cristina . Washington also sanctioned Panama-based Tentacool Commercial Inc., the registered owner of Gloria C , and Cuba-based Internacional Maritima SA, which owns Esperanza . Another Cuban shipping company, Petroleos Maritimos del Caribe S.A. (Petromarca), was designated alongside two vessels it manages: the LPG carrier Emilia and crude oil tanker Lourdes . Three of the five vessels were already listed under earlier Venezuela-related sanctions, while Emilia and Gloria C were newly added. The administration also targeted Guillermo Faustino Rodriguez Lopez Calleja, whom the State Department linked to a network of maritime shipping companies transporting petroleum products to and from Cuba. The sanctions come as Cuba continues to struggle with fuel shortages and electricity outages, making imported energy supplies increasingly important. Under the measures, property belonging to designated entities under U.S. jurisdiction is blocked, and U.S. persons are generally prohibited from conducting business with them. Foreign shipping operators and maritime service providers could also face additional sanctions exposure. articles.title: First gas gushes out of Southeast Asian deepwater project
articles.summary: This nearly $1-billion development has unlocked new deepwater reserves to boost energy security and stabilize power costs.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 6, 2026 · 1 day ago First gas gushes out of Southeast Asian deepwater project This nearly $1-billion development has unlocked new deepwater reserves to boost energy security and stabilize power costs. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 4 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Malampaya Source: Prime Energy Prime Energy Resources Development (Prime Energy), a subsidiary of Prime Infrastructure Capital, has brought fresh natural gas reserves online from deepwater Palawan to power the Luzon grid and strengthen national energy independence off the coast of the Philippines. The Malampaya Phase 4 (MP4) project has achieved its first gas milestone, bringing natural gas from the Malampaya East-1 and Camago-3 wells into the existing Malampaya production system and extending the productive life of the field. Prime Energy describes this achievement as a significant milestone for the Malampaya consortium that reinforces the project’s role in sustaining the Philippines’ indigenous natural gas supply. President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., together with Department of Energy (DOE) officials and SC 38 joint venture partners, witnessed the ceremonial first flow of gas at the Malampaya onshore gas plant in Batangas City on November 5. MP4 was completed in 27 months after the final investment decision, approximately five months ahead of its original schedule, and five months ahead of the industry benchmark, reflecting the strong coordination across the project, particularly given the complexity of deepwater development, which involved multiple contractors and suppliers and required the mobilization of specialized equipment, manufactured components, and technical experts from around the world. " For 25 years, Malampaya has demonstrated the value of developing our own energy resources. It has powered millions of Filipino households and businesses, supported economic growth, and generated more than $14 billion in government revenues. But Malampaya’s resources are finite. Sustaining production requires continued investment and the technical expertise to develop reserves that are increasingly challenging to access. That is what Malampaya Phase 4 represents. " — Enrique K. Razon Jr. Prime Infra Chairman MP4 marked the Philippines’ first offshore drilling campaign in more than a decade, with an international supply chain spanning 17 countries, including Germany, the United Kingdom, Norway, the Netherlands, the United States, Japan, South Korea, Australia, Singapore, Malaysia, and the Philippines. With an investment of close to a billion dollars, MP4 involved drilling two deepwater wells and installing subsea infrastructure to connect them to the existing Malampaya production platform. The project added an estimated 222 billion cubic feet (bcf) of recoverable natural gas reserves, capable of generating approximately 31.46 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity, enough to power 13.11 million Filipino households for one year. " — Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. President of the Philippines President Marcos also highlighted the importance of maximizing indigenous natural gas to help manage electricity costs, noting that greater use of Malampaya gas “could contribute to more competitive power rates because we are relying less on imported energy sources that are subject to volatile international energy prices.” The global network supported the fabrication, refurbishment, and delivery of critical subsea components and equipment, including umbilicals, valves, subsea systems, cables, generators, pipelines, and wellhead equipment. Philippine-based fabrication and manufacturing capabilities also contributed to the project, demonstrating the role of local industry in supporting complex offshore energy developments. Based on initial well-test results, the two wells will extend Malampaya’s productive life by approximately six years, depending on future gas offtake. Following first gas, the integration and ramp-up of the new wells into the existing production system will continue over the coming months. Sustainable production levels will be established as operating data becomes available. President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. (left) and Prime Infra Chairman Enrique K. Razon Jr. (right) mark the ceremonial First Gas flow of Malampaya Phase 4 (MP4) at the Malampaya Onshore Gas Plant in Batangas City on November 5. The project integrates two new deepwater wells to help secure the country’s grid stability. Malampaya natural gas currently supplies gas-fired power plants in Batangas that serve the Luzon grid. Additional indigenous gas from the new wells is expected to help sustain the domestic fuel supply for the power generation sector and support the country’s growing electricity requirements. A greater supply of indigenous natural gas can also help reduce the power sector’s exposure to fluctuations in international fuel markets. Over the past decade, domestic Malampaya gas has maintained a price advantage over imported spot liquefied natural gas (LNG), with the difference exceeding $4 per million British thermal units (Btu) at various points. This price advantage can help power generators manage fuel costs, although electricity rates remain subject to several factors, including generation costs, plant operations, market conditions, and applicable supply agreements, according to Prime Energy. The continued use of Malampaya gas at the SPPC power plant in Ilijan under an interim gas supply arrangement is also expected to contribute to an overall reduction in generation charges of gas-fired power plants, estimated to be approximately ₱0.36 per kilowatt-hour beginning September 1. The benefit underscores the value of access to domestic natural gas alongside imported LNG and other energy sources in diversifying the country’s fuel mix. A ceremonial flare lights up at the Malampaya Onshore Gas Plant, symbolizing the successful flow from Malampaya Phase 4. The milestone unlocks an estimated 222 billion cubic feet of natural gas reserves to power millions of Filipino homes. Since commercial operations began in 2001, the Malampaya Deep Water Gas-to-Power project has supplied natural gas to power plants in Batangas that support approximately one-fifth of Luzon’s electricity requirements, with its continued development set to help sustain this contribution as demand for reliable and affordable electricity grows. Beyond its contribution to the country’s energy supply, Malampaya has generated substantial economic value for the Philippines. Since production began in 2001, SC 38 has contributed more than $14 billion in revenues to the Philippine government. With MP4 now delivering gas from two new wells, Prime Energy continues to build on the Malampaya field’s legacy while pursuing further opportunities to develop the country’s indigenous energy resources. articles.body: Brent Oil Prices Prepare for Biggest Weekly Drop Since 2020 After US Midterms Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 6, 2026 © Adobe Stock/le Oil prices were set for a sharp weekly fall after the election losses of US President Donald Trump's Republican Party raised hopes of a de-escalation in the US-Israeli war on Iran and a stock market sell-off, though attacks on vessels in the Middle East continue to provide a floor to crude. In a whiplash see-saw session on Friday, Brent crude futures for January were up 26 cents, or 0.3%, at $98.55 a barrel by 1346 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures edged up by 57 cents, or 0.6%, to $91.09. The Brent contract is on track for a 16% decline this week, which would be its steepest weekly percentage fall since the start of the COVID-19 pandemic and its biggest in absolute terms in LSEG data going back to 1988. WTI is set for a 13% decline. The oil price slide comes against the backdrop of a dramatic rout in technology stocks. MKTS/GLOB A potential Iran war de-escalation could lead to more crude exports out of the region. Signs of an emerging supply excess amid demand destruction were reinforced by spot premiums for Middle Eastern crude benchmarks returning to levels reached before the conflict. “The crude market is loosening to a state of oversupply based on the balance, but the quality difference still exists as refiners recover what they can take versus what is available," said Rystad oil market analyst Janiv Shah, pointing to longer voyages and the need for ship-to-ship transfers as workarounds near Hormuz. "The market is still looking for evidence of a firm deal being signed (on Iran), or any backlash from either party could tighten fundamentals once more.” Oil prices fell 8% on Wednesday alone after the Democrats swept the US midterm elections, settling at two-month lows. However, prices rebounded on a surge in tanker attacks in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, renewing concerns over supply flows from the region. A Greek ship manager said on Friday that a seafarer was killed in a November 5 explosion on an oil products tanker in the Gulf, believed to have been caused by a missile attack. Data from Britain's maritime security agency UKMTO suggested that attacks on oil-carrying ships are still running at close to record pace. "Oil doesn't have to be at $117 to be expensive, and a fall to $93 doesn't mean the underlying problems have disappeared," said Matt Stanley from tanker trackers and energy flow analysts Kpler. "After over 25 years in this business, I honestly can't recall many weeks quite like this one." (Reuters)

PTTEP, TotalEnergies, KUFPEC, and Petronas’ farm-out agreements are related to joint investment in the SK410B Lang Lebah and B14 gas fields off the coast of Sarawak, offshore East Malaysia. The B14 gas field is located 14 kilometers from the Lang Lebah natural gas field under the Malaysia SK410B project. articles.body: Pipes November 6, 2026 · 1 day ago Tubular package provider selected for first commercial gas project off Cyprus NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Tenaris Luxembourg-headquartered Tenaris has secured contracts to supply oil country tubular goods (OCTG), line pipe and coating services for Cyprus's first-ever commercial gas development, operated by Eni in partnership with TotalEnergies. The deepwater Cronos project, located in Block 6, will be developed through a fast-track approach leveraging existing regional infrastructure. With resources estimated at more than 3 trillion cubic feet (85 billion cubic meters) of gas initially in place, the project is expected to reach a production plateau of up to 500 million standard cubic feet (14.2 million cubic meters) per day. The final investment decision (FID) was reached on July 28, and start-up is expected in H1 2028. Gas produced from the field will be transported to Egypt, where it will be processed through existing facilities, including the Zohr infrastructure, before being liquefied at the Damietta LNG plant for export to international markets, primarily Europe. Tenaris will deliver a coordinated supply scope for line pipe and OCTG solutions, supporting both the transportation infrastructure and offshore drilling requirements, and will supply seamless pipes for a 110-kilometer gas export pipeline and a monoethylene glycol (MEG) pipeline. The project will be executed under Tenaris’s One Line service model, which integrates pipe manufacturing, coating and logistics in a comprehensive pipeline solution. The seamless pipes will be manufactured at the company's Dalmine mill in Italy and supplied with buckle arrestors, as well as TenarisShawcor three-layer polypropylene (3LPP) anticorrosion coating applied at the company’s coating facility in Italy. For the offshore drilling scope, Tenaris will supply all tubular requirements. Part of the order will incorporate Dopeless technology, a mill-applied multifunctional coating, which the company says is designed to eliminate the need for thread compounds and simplify pipe handling and preparation while providing consistent lubrication during offshore running operations. “Being selected to provide OCTG together with offshore line pipe for Cronos demonstrates the value of our integrated tubular offering and our ability to support customers across different stages of complex offshore developments," said Alessandro D’Angelo , Commercial Vice President for OCTG Europe, C.I.S. and Sub-Saharan Africa. articles.body: Asia Dry Cargo Khalid Hashim set to pass the baton at Precious Shipping Adis Ajdin November 6, 2026 0 761 1 minute read Thailand’s Precious Shipping is preparing a change at the top, with longtime managing director Khalid Moinuddin Hashim moving to executive vice chairman and finance chief Gautam Khurana taking over the running of the Bangkok-listed dry bulk owner. The company’s board approved the leadership reshuffle, with both appointments taking effect on January 1, 2027, according to a filing with the Stock Exchange of Thailand. Khurana will continue to serve as director of finance until a successor is appointed. Both executives will retain their seats on the company’s board of directors and executive board. The transition marks a significant shift for Precious Shipping, which has been led by Hashim for more than three decades. He helped build the company into one of Thailand’s most prominent dry bulk owners following its establishment in 1989 and stock market listing in 1993. Khurana joined Precious in 2018 as chief financial officer before becoming finance director in 2019. His earlier career included a decade at DVB Bank in London and Singapore, where he worked in maritime finance, structured asset financing and leasing. The management shake-up comes amid a major fleet renewal programme that has seen Precious sell ageing handysize and supramax vessels while expanding its ultramax fleet. In September, the company returned to China’s Taizhou Sanfu Ship Engineering for four 64,500 dwt ultramax newbuildings worth a combined $141.8m, with deliveries scheduled between April 2030 and January 2031. The order followed an earlier $133.46m contract for four 63,500 dwt ultramaxes at the same yard, with two vessels already in service and the remaining pair due through the first quarter of 2027. Once the outstanding newbuildings arrive, Precious expects its fleet to reach 47 vessels totalling about 2.34m dwt. The owner has also started diversifying beyond dry bulk, entering the MR product tanker market earlier this year through direct acquisitions and its 45%-owned Nusantara Maritime joint venture. The NCS-01 project covers two areas in the Sea of Marmara and forms part of the government initiative to prepare prospective offshore wind sites for future development. The scope includes multibeam bathymetric surveys, side-scan sonar, sub-bottom profiling, magnetometer measurements, ultra-high-resolution seismic investigations and unexploded ordnance surveys. DenAr will also undertake offshore cone penetration testing and seabed sampling using its DP2 survey vessel DenAr Explorer , supported by laboratory testing and geotechnical reporting. The company has identified DenAr , DenAr Explorer , DenAr Surveyor and Salvor among the vessels being mobilised for the programme. The contract forms part of Turkey’s EU-supported Offshore Wind Energy Support Project, implemented with World Bank involvement. The programme also includes wind-resource measurements, feasibility assessments, grid-connection studies and environmental investigations covering prospective offshore wind development areas around Bandırma, Şarköy, and Karabiga. articles.body: Europe Tech Alfa Laval makes $700m NAVTOR bet Adis Ajdin November 6, 2026 0 635 2 minutes read Alfa Laval Alfa Laval Swedish industrial group Alfa Laval has struck a $700m all-cash deal to acquire Norwegian maritime software specialist NAVTOR, significantly expanding a digital shipping portfolio that already includes StormGeo and Portchain. The Stockholm-listed group has entered into a definitive agreement to buy NAVTOR for SEK6.85bn ($700m), with completion expected during the first quarter of 2027 subject to regulatory approvals. Alfa Laval described the purchase as one of the most significant transactions in its history. NAVTOR will join its Ocean Division, with its platform set to be brought together with StormGeo and Portchain to create a broader digital fleet offering spanning navigation, vessel performance, voyage optimisation and port operations. NAVTOR, founded in Egersund in 2011, employs around 400 people across 13 offices and serves customers in more than 90 countries. Alfa Laval said it expects the business to generate about $194m in revenue this year. “With this acquisition, Alfa Laval will expand its digital offering at a time when real-time decision-making is increasingly complex,” said chief executive Tom Erixon. NAVTOR has grown from an electronic navigation specialist into a wider ship-to-shore software business covering voyage planning, fleet monitoring, vessel performance, digital logbooks and onboard data workflows. Its expansion has also been driven by acquisitions. US technology investor Accel-KKR took a majority stake in NAVTOR in 2020, followed by purchases of performance analytics specialist Tres Solutions in 2021 and digital logbook developer Ingenium Marine in 2022. NAVTOR then combined with Voyager Worldwide in 2023, creating a business whose technology at the time served about 18,000 vessels. Alfa Laval has been assembling its own maritime software stack since buying weather routing and voyage optimisation company StormGeo for NOK3.63bn in 2021. That buildout accelerated again last week when StormGeo acquired Copenhagen-based Portchain, whose network links shipping lines with more than 200 container terminals accounting for over 40% of global container terminal capacity. The technology is being combined with StormGeo’s voyage optimisation tools so vessel speed and arrival decisions can respond to changing berth availability. NAVTOR brings another major layer to that strategy. SplashTech reported only last week that the company had added near-live AIS streaming to NavFleet, while earlier this year it expanded its digital logbook and compliance tools. Alfa Laval also disclosed that a recent NAVTOR internal review identified unspecified compliance matters, prompting the Norwegian company to strengthen its internal controls and compliance programme. The buyer said arrangements have been made to protect it against pre-acquisition liabilities connected with those matters. Erixon said Alfa Laval was confident the issues would be resolved. The acquisition will be funded through a mixture of Alfa Laval’s cash and existing financing programmes and is expected to be neutral to group margins in the short term. articles.title: Indian ship recycling breakthrough hits Brussels roadblock
articles.summary: A European Parliament committee has voted against allowing two Indian shipbreaking yards onto the EU’s approved recycling list, dealing a setback to shipowners pushing for greater access to South Asian dismantling capacity. The Parliament’s environment committee backed an objection this week to the European...
articles.body: Asia Europe Operations Regulatory Indian ship recycling breakthrough hits Brussels roadblock Adis Ajdin November 6, 2026 2 22,524 2 minutes read Leela Ship Recycling Leela Ship Recycling A European Parliament committee has voted against allowing two Indian shipbreaking yards onto the EU’s approved recycling list, dealing a setback to shipowners pushing for greater access to South Asian dismantling capacity. The Parliament’s environment committee backed an objection this week to the European Commission’s proposal to approve Shree Ram Vessel Scrap and YSI Recyclers, both located in the Alang-Sosiya shipbreaking hub in Gujarat. The two facilities had received preliminary backing from the Commission following inspections intended to establish whether they met the requirements of the EU Ship Recycling Regulation. Their inclusion would make them the first facilities on the Indian subcontinent to join the European list. MEPs opposing the proposal questioned whether yards using the beaching method, in which ships are dismantled on tidal shorelines, could adequately control pollution and hazardous waste. The objection also raised concerns about downstream waste handling, including scrap steel sent to local re-rolling mills that have not been assessed against EU industrial emissions standards. Environmental monitoring cited by campaigners showed elevated levels of toxic substances, including copper, chromium, cadmium and mercury, in the Alang-Sosiya area. “Today’s vote in the European Parliament sends a strong political message to the European Commission,” said Ingvild Jenssen, executive director of NGO Shipbreaking Platform, arguing that approving the facilities despite shortcomings identified during inspections would undermine the regulation’s environmental objectives. The vote puts lawmakers at odds with European shipping interests. Industry association ECSA had urged MEPs to support the Commission’s proposal, arguing that both yards had undergone extensive inspections and had been found compliant with EU standards. ECSA secretary general Sotiris Raptis warned that denying approval to facilities that had passed the assessment process would undermine the credibility of the regulation. Environmental organisations and recycling industry representatives have taken the opposite position, arguing that beaching operations cannot provide sufficient containment of hazardous materials and should not qualify for EU recognition. Campaigners have also challenged the industry’s argument that additional capacity is needed, pointing to more than 2m light displacement tonnes of combined annual capacity at facilities already on the EU list, which they claim is sufficient to handle recent recycling volumes involving EU-flagged and EU-owned ships. Under EU rules, EU-flagged commercial ships subject to the Ship Recycling Regulation must be dismantled at facilities on the approved European list. Opening that list to Indian yards would give owners more recycling options and potentially alter competition with existing approved facilities in Europe and Turkey. The committee vote is not a final rejection. The objection is expected to go before the full European Parliament later in November and does not automatically require the Commission to withdraw its proposal. Member states will also have a say in the approval process.
